explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The image depicts the life cycle of Human Papillomavirus (HPV) in the stratified squamous epithelium, showing infection of basal cells, viral DNA replication in the stratum spinosum, and assembly of viral particles in the upper epithelial layers.

HPV is a non-enveloped, double-stranded DNA virus belonging to the Papillomaviridae family.

Certain HPV types (16, 18, 31, 33, 45, etc.) are high-risk oncogenic viruses, causing:

  • Cervical carcinoma
  • Anal carcinoma
  • Oropharyngeal carcinoma
  • Penile, vulvar, and vaginal cancers

HPV is a well-known oncogenic (cancer-causing) virus (Option B).

  • HPV is a small, non-enveloped, circular dsDNA virus (Option A ruled out).
  • High-risk strains (16, 18): These are responsible for approximately 70% of Cervical Cancers. They also cause anal, vulvar, vaginal, and oropharyngeal cancers.
  • Mechanism: Viral oncoproteins E6 and E7 bind to and inhibit host tumor suppressor proteins p53 and pRb, respectively, leading to uncontrolled cell proliferation.

HPV typically causes painless warts (condyloma acuminata) or asymptomatic latent infections. (Option D ruled out)

  • Painful genital ulcers are characteristic of Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV) or Haemophilus ducreyi (Chancroid).

Coordination of life cycle of virus with epidermal cell differentiation:

  • Basal Layer: Initial infection and maintenance of viral DNA.
  • Stratum Spinosum/Granulosum: Replication of viral DNA and expression of early genes.
  • Stratum Corneum: Assembly of capsid proteins and release of infectious virus particles.

Most common low-risk types: 6 and 11 (Genital Warts/Respiratory Papillomatosis).

Cytology hallmark: Koilocytes (squamous epithelial cells with a perinuclear halo and wrinkled "raisinoid" nucleus) on a Pap smear.

A highly effective HPV vaccine (e.g., Gardasil 9) is available. It is ideally administered to adolescents before they become sexually active to prevent cervical cancer and genital warts. (Option C ruled out)



Reference:

Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology, 11th Edition, Pages 418-419, 511

Explanation:

Long-term inhaled corticosteroids cause local immunosuppression, predisposing to oropharyngeal candidiasis, which presents as whitish, scrapable plaques over the palate and tonsils.

Oral lichen planus(Option A): Characterized by reticulated lacy white lines (Wickham striae) on buccal mucosa, often bilateral and symmetric. Lesions are non-scrapable and may be associated with chronic immune-mediated mucocutaneous disease.

[[figure-2]]

Aphthous ulcer(Option C): Also known as recurrent aphthous stomatitis, presents as painful shallow ulcers with a yellow/grey base and erythematous halo, commonly on non-keratinized mucosa (buccal mucosa, inner lips, floor of mouth). They are not white plaques, not scrapable, and do not show Wickham striae, making them inconsistent with fungal or hyperkeratotic lesions.

[[figure-3]]

Leukoplakia(Option D): Represents a white, non-scrapable premalignant epithelial lesion linked to chronic tobacco or alcohol exposure. Unlike infectious plaques, leukoplakia is persistent, asymptomatic, and lacks associated erythema or pseudomembrane. No scrapability and no acute inflammatory features differentiate it from candidiasis.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • This patient is demonstrating treatment failure on ciprofloxacin.
  • In the current clinical landscape (especially in South Asia), many strains of Salmonella typhi have developed resistance to fluoroquinolones (Nalidixic Acid Resistant Salmonella typhi or NARST).
  • Third-generation cephalosporins like ceftriaxone are the drug of choice for severe or resistant enteric fever, especially in toxic patients.
  • Enteric fever caused by Salmonella Typhi has shifted toward multidrug-resistant (MDR) strains (resistant to chloramphenicol, ampicillin, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole).
  • Many isolates also show reduced fluoroquinolone susceptibility, detected clinically by nalidixic acid resistance (NaR)
    • NaR isolates respond poorly to ofloxacin regimens - higher failure rates and prolonged fever clearance times.
    • Alternatives for resistant typhoid include:
      • Ceftriaxone
      • Cefixime
      • Azithromycin

Chloramphenicol and Ampicillin (Option A and B): These were traditional first-line treatments. However, they are no longer used empirically because of the high prevalence of Multidrug-Resistant (MDR) typhoid, which is defined as resistance to chloramphenicol, ampicillin, and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole.

Doxycycline (Option D): Tetracyclines are not effective against Salmonella typhi and have no established role in the treatment of enteric fever.

The bluish-white lesions described are Koplik spots, which are pathognomonic for measles and appear before the rash. Measles presents with fever, cough, coryza, conjunctivitis, followed by a cephalocaudal maculopapular rash.

Features

Description

Etiology

Measles virus (Paramyxoviridae), negative-sense ssRNA

Rash

Erythematous maculopapular rash starting at the hairline, spreading cephalocaudally and centrifugally, becomes confluent

Koplik Spots

Bluish-white enanthem on buccal mucosa opposite molars; pathognomonic, appears before the rash

Prodrome (3 C’s)

Cough, Coryza, Conjunctivitis with high fever and malaise

Transmission

Highly contagious respiratory droplets and airborne spread; peak infectivity during prodrome and early rash

Mumps (Option B): Mumps primarily affects salivary glands, especially parotid glands. Its Oral findings include, parotid duct erythema (Stensen duct), not Koplik spots.

Chickenpox (Option C): In chickenpox, rash is vesicular, not maculopapular. Lesions are in different stages of healing (dew drop on a rose petal). No specific buccal mucosal sign like Koplik spots.

Rubella (Option D): Viral illness that features Forchheimer spots on the soft palate, not Koplik spots, and usually has a milder rash compared to measles.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

An HIV patient with dry cough, progressive weight loss, and generalized weakness suggests chronic pulmonary disease with constitutional symptoms, which is characteristic of tuberculosis. HIV-induced immunosuppression increases the risk of reactivation and disseminated TB.

Histoplasma capsulatum (Option A): It usually presents with pulmonary or disseminated disease with fever, hepatosplenomegaly, and can mimic TB, but a dry cough alone is less typical without systemic fungal features.

Candida albicans (Option B): It primarily causes oral thrush, esophagitis, or vaginal candidiasis in HIV patients. Pulmonary candidiasis is rare, and Candida does not typically present with a chronic dry cough.

Pneumocystis jirovecii (Option C): It causes acute/subacute dyspnea, hypoxemia, and dry cough, with ground-glass infiltrates, but significant weight loss and chronic constitutional symptoms point more toward TB rather than PCP.

Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology, 11th Edition, Page 264.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Immunity is the resistance exhibited by the host towards injury caused by microorganisms and their products. It is broadly classified into two main types.

Type of Immunity

Description

Natural Active Immunity

Develops when the host’s immune system responds to a natural infection (clinical or subclinical). The body produces its own antibodies and memory cells in response to the live pathogen.

Natural Passive Immunity

Occurs by transfer of ready-made antibodies from mother to fetus/infant. IgG crosses the placenta, and IgA is provided through colostrum and breast milk. Protection is temporary, and no immune memory is formed.

Artificial Active Immunity

Induced by vaccination (e.g., BCG, MMR). Vaccines introduce killed or attenuated pathogens or antigens, stimulating the body to produce its own antibodies and immunological memory.

Artificial Passive Immunity

Achieved by administration of pre-formed antibodies (e.g., anti-tetanus serum). It provides immediate but short-term protection, with no antibody production or memory by the recipient.


Reference:

Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology, 10th Edition, Pages 83 - 86.

correctAnswer: B. IgG2 deficiency is frequently associated with infections with encapsulated bacteria
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

IgG2 is important for antibody response against polysaccharide capsules of bacteria (e.g., Streptococcus pneumoniae). Its deficiency causes recurrent infections with encapsulated organisms and often coexists with IgA deficiency.

IgG (Immunoglobulin G) is the most abundant class of serum immunoglobulin (about 80%). It is the only maternal antibody that crosses the placenta, providing natural passive immunity to the newborn.

IgG (Immunoglobulin G) Subclasses

IgG1 (65%)
  • Most abundant
  • Responds to protein antigens
  • Strong in opsonization

IgG2 (23%)
  • Most clinically important here
  • Targets polysaccharide capsules of bacteria
  • Deficiency → recurrent infections with encapsulated bacteria
    (e.g., Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae)
  • Associated with IgA deficiency

IgG3 (8%)
  • Long hinge region
  • Strong complement activator
  • Important in viral & protein antigen response

IgG4 (4%)
  • Linked to chronic allergen exposure
  • Does NOT activate complement effectively

IgG1 deficiency is the most common and is linked to IgA deficiency (Option A): While IgG1 is the most abundant subclass, its isolated deficiency is rare. Selective IgA deficiency is the most common primary immunodeficiency overall, not IgG1 deficiency.

IgG3 deficiency is the commonest cause of pyogenic infections in children (Option C): IgG3 is an effective opsonin and complement activator, but IgG2 deficiency is more specifically associated with the inability to tackle the polysaccharide capsules of pyogenic bacteria.

IgG4 deficiency causes anaphylaxis with IgA-containing transfusions (Option D): IgA deficiency, not IgG4 deficiency, causes anaphylaxis with IgA-containing transfusions.



Reference:

Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology, 10th Edition, Page 99

question: Which of the following statements is most accurate regarding IgG subclass deficiencies?

correctAnswer: B. Isotypes are found in the constant regions; idiotypes are found in the variable regions.
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Antigenic determinants of immunoglobulins are classified into three types:

Types

Description

Isotypes

These are shared by all members of a species. They define the antibody class (e.g., IgG, IgM, IgA, IgE, IgD) and light chain types (Kappa, Lambda).

Location: Found in the constant regions of heavy and light chains

Allotypes

These are allelic variants that differ between individuals of the same species. They are inherited as Mendelian traits (e.g., Gm markers on IgG).

Location: Found in the constant regions, specifically involving subtle amino acid differences.

Idiotypes

These are unique to a single antibody clone produced by a specific B-cell. The total of idiotope determinants on an Ig molecule constitutes its idiotype.

Location: Found in the variable regions (Hypervariable regions or CDRs) of the Fab fragment.

Isotypes are unique to an antibody clone; idiotypes are shared by all members of a species (Option A): These definitions are reversed; isotypes are species-wide class markers, while idiotypes are unique "signatures" of a specific antibody clone's antigen-binding site.

Isotypes are genetic alleles varying between individuals; idiotypes define the antibody class (Option C): Describes allotypes as isotypes. Isotypes define the antibody class for the entire species.

Isotypes are only on the Fab fragment; idiotypes are located on the Fc fragment (Option D): Idiotypes are part of the antigen-binding site (Fab), whereas isotypes are primarily determined by the constant regions of the heavy chains (Fc and part of Fab).



Reference:

Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology, 10th Edition, Page 101-102.

Explanation:

Chronic Granulomatous Disease: Impairment of phagocytic cell function.

  • Normal immunoglobulin levels, T cells, B cells, and phagocytic cell counts.
  • Genetic mutation in cytochrome b-558.
    • Phagocytes cannot produce superoxide and peroxide, leading to impaired microbial killing.

Diagnostic Tests for CGD

Nitroblue Tetrazolium (NBT) Test
  • Principle: NBT dye is reduced by superoxide → forms blue formazan
  • Result:
    • Normal: Blue color (positive test)
    • CGD: No color change - defective oxidative burst (negative test)
  • Limitation: Qualitative, less sensitive

Dihydrorhodamine (DHR) Flow Cytometry Test (Gold Standard)
  • Principle: DHR is oxidized to fluorescent rhodamine during oxidative burst
  • Result:
    • Normal: High fluorescence
    • CGD: Reduced/absent fluorescence
  • Advantages:
    • More sensitive and quantitative than NBT
    • Can detect carrier states (especially in X-linked CGD)
    • Preferred modern diagnostic test.

Coombs test (Option A) detects antibodies against red blood cells and is used in autoimmune hemolytic anemia, not for neutrophil function.

ELISA for IgG (Option C): ELISA measures antibody levels in the blood and does not assess neutrophil oxidative burst activity.

Complement fixation test (Option D) evaluates the presence of antibodies and complement activity, not phagocyte oxidative metabolism.



Reference:

Jawetz, Melnick, & Adelberg's Medical Microbiology, 28th Edition, Page 148.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

In Wiskott-Aldrich Syndrome, cellular immunity is defective.

  • The transfer of cell-mediated immunity using sensitized donor lymphocytes or their dialysable extracts (transfer factor) is called adoptive immunity.
  • It involves the transfer of immune competence from an immunized individual to a non-immune or immunodeficient individual.

Transfer Factor

Definition

A low-molecular-weight, dialyzable extract obtained from sensitized T-lymphocytes (specifically from the disruption of these cells).

Core Function

It "transfers" specific cell-mediated immunity (CMI) and delayed-type hypersensitivity (DTH) from an immune donor to a non-immune recipient.

Chemical Nature

A heat-stable, peptide-ribonucleotide complex; it is not an antibody or an immunoglobulin.

Clinical Significance

Treat patients with defective T-cell immunity, such as those with certain chronic fungal infections or specific immunodeficiency syndromes.

Natural Active Immunity (Option A): Immunity developed after natural infection; the body produces its own antibodies and T cells.

Artificial Active Immunity (Option B): Immunity induced by vaccination; the host actively forms an immune response and memory.

Natural Passive Immunity (Option D): Transfer of maternal antibodies (IgG via placenta, IgA via colostrum); immediate but temporary protection.



Reference:

Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology, 10th Edition, Page 86
question: A patient with Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome receives a dialysable extract from sensitized donor lymphocytes to correct a specific defect in cellular immunity. This therapeutic transfer of cell-mediated immunity is known as:

The image shows Staphylococcus aureus → Cocci in clusters (Grape-like).

  • While all Staphylococci are Catalase-positive, the Coagulase test is the definitive marker used to distinguish S. aureus (Coagulase-positive) from Coagulase-negative Staphylococci (CoNS) like S. epidermidis, which are common skin commensals.
  • The enzyme coagulase acts with a plasma factor to convert fibrinogen to a fibrin clot.

[[figure-1]]

Catalase test (Option A) differentiates staphylococci (catalase-positive) from streptococci (catalase-negative) but cannot distinguish S. aureus from other staphylococci.

Optochin sensitivity test (Option C) is specifically used to identify Streptococcus pneumoniae (sensitive) from Viridans group streptococci (resistant). These organisms appear in pairs or chains, not clusters.

Bacitracin sensitivity test (Option D) is used to differentiate Group A Streptococcus from other beta-hemolytic streptococci, not staphylococci.

Jawetz, Melnick, & Adelberg's Medical Microbiology, 28th Edition, Page 45.

Explanation:

The clinical presentation of leonine facies and extensive nerve involvement in the presence of acid-fast bacilli (AFB) is diagnostic of Lepromatous Leprosy, caused by Mycobacterium Leprae/Hansen's Bacillus.

Type

  • Obligate intracellular - Can't grow on culture media (Statement 1)
  • Obligate aerobe (Statement 4)

Transmission

Nasal droplet > Contact > Breast milk

Specimen

Slit skin smear (6 samples):

  • 4 skin (Forehead, cheek, chin, buttock)
  • 1 ear lobe
  • 1 nasal mucosa

Biopsy

Thickened peripheral nerves

Stain

Fite-Faraco stain (5% H₂SO₄)

Microscopy (lepromatous leprosy)

Bacilli + Virchow cell (macrophages packed with cigar-shaped bacilli - globi) (Statement 2)

[[figure-1]]

Antibody

Against PGL (phenolic glycolipid)

Prognosis

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Management:

  • Surgical Debridement: Immediate and aggressive removal of all necrotic tissue is mandatory. Since the fungus causes vascular thrombosis, systemic drugs cannot reach dead tissue; surgery clears the path and reduces the fungal load.
  • High-Dose Antifungals: Intravenous Liposomal Amphotericin B is the first-line medical treatment. It must be started as soon as the diagnosis is suspected. Isavuconazole or Posaconazole are alternative or step-down options.

question: A 27-year-old man presents with fever and shortness of breath. A fungating mass is seen in the right lung. Histopathology from the mass with modified Grocott’s silver methanamnine stain is given below. Identify the organism.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Dermatophytosis, also known as tinea or ringworm, is a superficial fungal infection limited to keratinised tissues (skin, hair, nails) and is not acquired through traumatic implantation like thorn pricks. It is usually transmitted through direct contact with infected humans, animals, or fomites. They are typically of the Trichophyton, Microsporum, or Epidermophyton type. Risk factors include using public showers, contact sports such as wrestling, excessive sweating, contact with animals, obesity, and poor immune function.

Incorrect Options:

Sporotrichosis (Option A): Sporotrichosis is classically known as "rose gardener’s disease" and commonly follows traumatic implantation of Sporothrix schenckii through a thorn prick, forming noduloulcerative lesions along lymphatics.

Chromoblastomycosis (Option B): Chromoblastomycosis is caused by pigmented fungi that enter through traumatic injuries, especially thorn pricks or splinters, leading to chronic nodular, cauliflower-like, verrucous, cicatricial or mixed lesions showing medlar/muriform/sclerotic/copper-penny bodies on histopathology.

Mycetoma (Option C): Mycetoma (both actinomycetoma and eumycetoma) follows traumatic implantation of organisms into deeper tissues, often through thorns or sharp objects, particularly in farmers walking barefoot.

explanationHtml:

When incubated in serum at 37°C for 2 hours, C. albicans produces germ tubes, which appear as filamentous outgrowths with no constriction at their point of origin.

Incorrect Options:

Candida krusei (Option B): C. krusei does not form germ tubes. It typically shows elongated blastoconidia and pseudohyphae but lacks true germ tube formation.

Candida tropicalis (Option C): Although C. tropicalis can form pseudohyphae, it produces constricted outgrowths (not true germ tubes), so the germ tube test is negative.

Cryptococcus neoformans (Option D): This yeast is encapsulated and never forms germ tubes. It shows a prominent polysaccharide capsule and is diagnosed by India ink staining, not germ tube testing.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Improperly canned food contains preformed botulinum toxin that is ingested and absorbed, leading to descending flaccid paralysis. This represents vehicle-borne transmission, where contaminated food or water acts as the vehicle. Example: Botulism from canned foods, cholera from contaminated water.

Direct transmission(Option A):

  • Requires person-to-person contact, but botulism is not contagious. Example: Influenza, COVID-19, gonorrhea (spread via direct contact).

Indirect transmission(Option B):

  • Involves fomites (objects that carry pathogens), which do not transmit botulinum toxin in foodborne cases. Example: The common cold spreads via contaminated doorknobs or surfaces.

Vector-borne transmission(Option D):

  • Requires insects or arthropods, none of which are involved in botulism.

Example: Malaria via the Anopheles mosquito, plague via the rat flea.

question: A patient develops acute flaccid paralysis after consuming improperly canned food the previous day. The illness is attributed to Clostridium botulinum toxin. What is the mode of transmission in this case?

correctAnswer: A. Long-term antifungal therapy with surgical debridement
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The findings of chronic foot swelling with multiple discharging sinuses and hyphae on biopsy point towards the diagnosis of Eumycetoma, a chronic subcutaneous fungal infection. The management consists of prolonged antifungal therapy combined with surgical debridement.

Clinical features: Eumycetoma classically presents with a triad of:

  1. Painless subcutaneous nodular swelling
  2. Multiple discharging sinuses
  3. Grains (fungal granules) in the discharge
    There is a gradual progression with fibrosis, induration (woody foot), and potential bone involvement causing deformity.
  4. Biopsy: Tissue biopsy reveals fungal grains composed of septate branching hyphae, often surrounded by Splendore Hoeppli phenomenon (eosinophilic material). On special stains, hyphae are highlighted by PAS and GMS stains.

[[figure-1]]

Treatment:
Management of Eumycetoma is difficult due to deep fibrosis and slow fungal proliferation, hence it requires a combined and prolonged approach:

  • Long-term antifungal therapy: Itraconazole (first-line), Ketoconazole, or Posaconazole given for 6-18 months or longer.
  • Surgical debridement: Performed to remove necrotic and granular tissue, reduce fungal load, and enhance penetration of antifungal drugs. This combined approach is considered standard of care.

Immediate amputation (Option B): Reserved for advanced, refractory disease only.

Short-term antifungal therapy (Option C): It is inadequate due to poor drug penetration.

Antibiotics (Option D): It is effective only for actinomycetoma, not fungal disease.

Co-trimoxazole + Amikacin

Co-trimoxazole duration: 6-12 months.Amikacin duration: Given in cycles of 21 days ON / 21 days OFF, for several cycles (commonly 2-6 months total depending on response)



Reference:

Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology, 11th Edition, Pages 535-536.

question: A 30-year-old farmer presents with chronic fatigue and microcytic hypochromic anemia. Stool examination reveals the egg shown in the image. Which of the following serves as the definitive host for this parasite?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Paratenic host (also known as a transport host) is one in which the parasite survives and remains infective, but does not undergo further development.
  • In the case of Diphyllobothrium latum (fish tapeworm), large predator fish consume smaller infected fish. The plerocercoid larvae then migrate to the tissues of the larger fish and await ingestion by a definitive host.

Types of Host

Definitive host

Parasite undergoes its sexual cycle or reaches adult maturity (e.g., Man for Diphyllobothrium latum) (Option A ruled out).

Intermediate host

Parasite undergoes asexual reproduction or essential larval development (e.g., Cyclops - 1st intermediate host; small fish - 2nd intermediate host for D. latum) (Option B ruled out).

Reservoir host

Animal host that maintains the parasite's life cycle in nature and serves as a source of infection for humans (e.g., Dogs or cats for Diphyllobothrium latum) (Option D ruled out).

Paratenic host

Parasite survives and remains infective, but does not undergo further development (e.g., large predatory fish in D. latum). (Option C)

Paniker’s Textbook of Medical Parasitology, 8th Edition, Page 1-2.
question: In the life cycle of the fish tapeworm, a large predatory fish that consumes smaller infected fish and harbors the plerocercoid larva without any further development acts as which type of host?

explanationHtml:
Option C: Penetration of skin

  • The patient has Ancylostoma duodenale (hookworm) infestation based on the clinical scenario.
  • Filariform larva enters the human body by penetration of the skin.
  • It causes iron deficiency anaemia [0.2 ml/day/worm blood sucked].
  • Host – Man.
  • Infective form – 3rd stage filariform (L3) larva.
  • Mode of transmission- penetration of the skin by 3rd stage filariform (L3) larva (by walking barefoot in dampened soil).
  • Habitat- small intestine.

[[figure-1]]

EGG - Segmentation is seen [Blastomeres]:

[[figure-2]]

  • Using a microscope, the standard method for diagnosing hookworm infestation is by identifying hookworm eggs in a stool sample.

Chandler Index:

  • Used for hookworm.
  • The average number of hookworm eggs per gram of faeces for the entire community.
  • Below 200 -Hookworm is not much significant.
  • 200 – 250 -May be regarded as a potential danger.
  • 250 – 300 -Minor public health problem.
  • Above 300 -Important public health problem.

Option A: Ingestion

  • The ingestion of pathogenic organisms may occur due to contaminated food or water and by licking or chewing on contaminated objects or surfaces.
  • The following diseases are caused by ingestion worldwide:
    • Norovirus
    • Salmonella
    • Clostridium perfringens
    • Campylobacter
    • Staphylococcus aureus (Staph)

Option B: Inhalation

    • Silicosis
    • Byssinosis or brown lung disease
    • Hypersensitivity pneumonitis

Option D: Inoculation

    • Diphtheria

question: A 35-year-old male presents with vague abdominal pain and reports passing white, flat, ribbon-like segments in his stool. To which of the following classes of helminthes does the causative agent belong?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Strongyloides stercoralis is a facultative parasite → Capable of leading both a parasitic and a free-living existence depending on the environmental conditions.

Classification of Parasites

Ectoparasite

Lives on the outer surface of the host without penetrating tissues (e.g., Pediculus humanus).

Endoparasite

Lives inside the body of the host (e.g., Entamoeba histolytica).

Obligate parasite

Completely dependent on the host and cannot lead a free-living life (e.g., Plasmodium species). (Option A ruled out)

Facultative parasite

Capable of leading both a parasitic and a free-living existence (e.g., Strongyloides stercoralis). (Option B)

Accidental parasite

Infects a host where it does not ordinarily live (e.g., Echinococcus granulosus in humans). (Option C ruled out)

Aberrant parasite

Infects a host where it cannot undergo further development (e.g., Toxocara canis in humans). (Option D ruled out)

Paniker’s Textbook of Medical Parasitology, 8th Edition, Page 1.
question: What type of parasite is Strongyloides stercoralis?

correctAnswer: B. Malabsorption due to adherence of trophozoites to the small intestinal mucosa
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The video demonstrates the characteristic "falling leaf" motility of Giardia lamblia trophozoites, a distinctive feature seen on fresh stool wet mount microscopy.
  • Giardia lamblia is a flagellated protozoan transmitted through the fecal-oral route, commonly by ingestion of contaminated water.
  • It is one of the most common causes of waterborne diarrheal illness worldwide.
  • After excystation in the duodenum, trophozoites attach to the duodenal and proximal jejunal mucosa using their ventral adhesive disc.
  • They do not invade the intestinal mucosa but instead interfere with brush border enzyme activity and nutrient absorption, resulting in malabsorption.
  • Patients typically present with greasy, foul-smelling stools (steatorrhea), abdominal bloating, flatulence, weight loss, and fat-soluble vitamin deficiency, particularly after drinking untreated water.

Invasion and ulceration of the colonic mucosa (Option A) is the characteristic pathogenic mechanism of Entamoeba histolytica, which invades the colonic epithelium and produces flask-shaped ulcers, leading to dysentery. Giardia lamblia remains confined to the lumen of the small intestine and does not invade the mucosa.

Production of an enterotoxin causing secretory diarrhea (Option C) is the mechanism of organisms such as Vibrio cholerae and enterotoxigenic Escherichia coli (ETEC). These pathogens stimulate intestinal secretion without causing malabsorption. Giardia causes diarrhea through impaired absorption rather than toxin production.

Hematogenous dissemination to the liver forming abscesses (Option D) is a well-recognized complication of Entamoeba histolytica, which may spread via the portal circulation to produce amoebic liver abscesses. Giardia lamblia does not invade tissues or disseminate beyond the intestinal lumen, making this option incorrect.



Reference:
  • https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37247374/
  • https://www.nejm.org/doi/abs/10.1056/NEJMicm2211056

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Agents

Mechanism of Action

Phenols

Act by disrupting the cell membrane, which leads to the leakage of intracellular contents. At higher concentrations, they also cause the irreversible precipitation of cellular proteins.

Glutaraldehyde

Works by alkylating the chemical groups (amino, carboxyl, hydroxyl, and sulfhydryl) of proteins and nucleic acids. This structural alteration effectively kills bacteria, spores, and viruses.

Halogens

Chlorine and its compounds (like hypochlorites) release nascent oxygen or form hypochlorous acid, which oxidizes the essential sulfhydryl (-SH) groups of enzymes. This inhibits vital metabolic processes within the microbe.

Alcohols (like 70% ethanol)

Act by denaturing bacterial proteins and acting as lipid solvents. By dissolving the lipid components of the cell membrane, they cause rapid cell lysis.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Standard (conventional) PCR is used for double-stranded DNA.
  • RT-PCR (Reverse Transcriptase PCR) is specifically designed to amplify RNA sequences (such as mRNA or RNA viral genomes), not double-stranded DNA.
  • In RT-PCR, the enzyme Reverse Transcriptase (RT) is used to synthesize a complementary DNA (cDNA) strand from the RNA template. Once the cDNA is created, it undergoes the standard PCR cycles (Denaturation, Annealing, and Extension) for exponential amplification. This method is the gold standard for detecting RNA viruses like H1N1 or SARS-CoV-2.

It is important to distinguish between Reverse Transcriptase PCR (RT-PCR) and Real-Time PCR (qPCR), as they serve different purposes despite often being used together.

[[figure-1]]

It utilizes an enzyme to create a DNA copy from an RNA strand (Option B): In RT-PCR, the enzyme reverse transcriptase first synthesizes complementary DNA (cDNA) from an RNA template.

The exponential amplification phase of the process uses the newly synthesized cDNA as a template (Option C): The newly formed cDNA then serves as the template for amplification by standard PCR.

It is a critical diagnostic tool for identifying RNA viruses such as the H1N1 Influenza virus (Option D): RT-PCR is commonly used for the detection of RNA viruses, for example, the H1N1 virus from nasopharyngeal swab samples.



Reference:

Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology, 10th Edition, Page 664

Quellung Reaction

  • Rheumatic heart disease
  • Prosthetic valves

Prophylaxis

Antibiotic prophylaxis (e.g., amoxicillin) before dental procedures in high-risk patients

Secretion of hyaluronidase to digest tooth protein matrix (Option B): Hyaluronidase is not involved in dental caries; it aids tissue invasion in other streptococcal infections.

Direct invasion of dentin by bacterial cells (Option C): Dental caries is caused by acid-mediated demineralization, not direct bacterial invasion of dentin. Bacteria may digest the dentin protein matrix later, but initiation occurs via acid.

question: A 28-year-old male presenting with epigastric pain and weight loss reports a history of consuming measly pork, with stool examination revealing the egg shown in the image. Which of the following is true regarding the causative agent?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:
The life cycle shown in the image corresponds to the fish tapeworm, Diphyllobothrium latum, which involves humans as the definitive host, freshwater copepods as the first intermediate host, and fish as the second intermediate host.

Requires three hosts to complete its cycle:

  • Definitive Host: Man (and other fish-eating mammals) harboring the adult worm in the small intestine.
  • First Intermediate Host: Freshwater crustaceans (Cyclops or Diaptomus), where the procercoid larva develops.
  • Second Intermediate Host: Freshwater fish, where the larva transforms into the plerocercoid (sparganum) stage.

Infective Form: Plerocercoid larva is the infective stage for humans, acquired by ingesting raw or undercooked freshwater fish.

[[figure-1]]

Pork tapeworm (Taenia solium) (Option A): Humans acquire it from undercooked pork, and pigs, not fish, are the intermediate host.

Dwarf tapeworm (Hymenolepis nana) (Option B): Has a direct life cycle and does not require fish as an intermediate host.

Dog tapeworm/Hydatid tapeworm (Echinococcus granulosus) (Option D): Causes hydatid disease in dogs as definitive hosts and does not involve fish.



Reference:

Paniker’s Textbook of Medical Parasitology, 8th Edition, Page 118-120.

question: Identify the egg:

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The colposcopy image demonstrates multiple, focal, punctate macular hemorrhages on the cervical mucosa, a characteristic strawberry cervix appearance, known as colpitis macularis.
  • This sign is specific for infection with the flagellated, flagellar-motile protozoan Trichomonas vaginalis.
  • Other findings seen are:
    • Desquamation of vaginal epithelium
    • Metaplastic changes

Candida albicans infection (Option A) is a dimorphic opportunist fungus that causes vulvovaginal candidiasis, characterized by a thick, white, cottage cheese-like vaginal discharge, intense pruritus, and vulvovaginal erythema without punctate cervical macular hemorrhages.

Bacterial vaginosis (Option C) is a synergistic, non-inflammatory dysbiosis characterized by a depletion of normal lactobacilli and overgrowth of anaerobes (Gardnerella vaginalis), presenting with a thin, homogeneous, grayish-white vaginal discharge and a positive whiff test, without cervical capillary hemorrhages.

Neisseria gonorrhoea infection (Option D) is a Gram-negative intracellular diplococcus that typically causes acute mucopurulent cervicitis, presenting with a highly friable, easily bleeding cervix and thick purulent endocervical discharge, rather than the distinct punctate capillary lesions of a strawberry cervix.



Reference:

Paniker's Textbook of Medical Parasitology, 8th Edition, Page 37.
question: A colposcopy image is given. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The patient’s chronic cough, hemoptysis, ring-shaped lung opacities, cystic lesions on CT, and operculated eggs in sputum strongly indicate Paragonimus westermani (lung fluke) infection.

Humans acquire the infection by ingesting raw, salted, or undercooked freshwater crabs or crayfish containing infective metacercariae.

Praziquantel is the universally recommended first-line drug of choice for both pulmonary and extrapulmonary paragonimiasis due to its excellent efficacy and tolerability.

Clinical Presentation:

  • Pulmonary paragonimiasis
    • Fibrous lung cysts communicating with bronchi
    • Cough, chest pain, hemoptysis
    • Sputum contains golden-brown operculated eggs
    • Eosinophilia
    • Can mimic pulmonary tuberculosis
  • Extrapulmonary paragonimiasis
    • Abdominal: Hepatomegaly, abdominal pain, bloody diarrhea
    • Cerebral: Headache, fever, paralysis, visual disturbances, seizures

Ivermectin (Option A) is used for strongyloidiasis and onchocerciasis. It has no role in fluke (trematode) infections.

Diethylcarbamazine (DEC)(Option B) is the drug of choice for filariasis (Wuchereria bancrofti).

Albendazole (Option D) is effective for many nematode infections (e.g., ascariasis, neurocysticercosis).



Reference:

Paniker's Textbook of Medical Parasitology, 8th Edition, Pages 160-162.

During daytime or when they are absent from peripheral blood, microfilariae tend to sequester in the pulmonary capillaries. This pulmonary sequestration explains their decreased daytime detectability in peripheral blood smears.

correctAnswer: A. Motile, pear-shaped flagellated trophozoite with an undulating membrane
explanationHtml:
Frothy green vaginal discharge with vulvovaginal irritation is characteristic of trichomoniasis caused by Trichomonas vaginalis. Elevated vaginal pH supports the diagnosis. Wet mount microscopy classically demonstrates motile pear-shaped flagellated trophozoites with an undulating membrane.

Trichomoniasis:

  • Sexually transmitted protozoal infection caused by Trichomonas vaginalis.
  • Common features include frothy yellow-green vaginal discharge, pruritus, dysuria, and dyspareunia.
  • Vaginal pH is usually >4.5.
  • “Strawberry cervix” may occur due to punctate cervical haemorrhages.
  • Wet mount examination shows motile trophozoites.

Clinical differentiation of common causes of vaginitis:

  • Frothy green discharge, motile trophozoites - trichomoniasis.
  • Thick curdy white discharge, pseudohyphae - candidiasis.
  • Thin grey discharge, fishy odour, clue cells - bacterial vaginosis.
  • Purulent cervicitis, intracellular diplococci - gonorrhea.

Budding yeast cells with pseudohyphae (Option B): Seen in vulvovaginal candidiasis caused by Candida albicans. Usually presents with thick curdy white discharge and normal vaginal pH.

Intracellular Gram-negative diplococci within neutrophils (Option C): Characteristic of gonorrhoea caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Typically causes cervicitis rather than frothy discharge.

Clue cells with adherent coccobacilli (Option D): Seen in bacterial vaginosis caused by Gardnerella vaginalis. Associated with a positive whiff test and fishy odour.



Reference:

Ananthanarayan and Paniker’s Textbook of Microbiology, 11th Edition, Page 590.

question: A 28-year-old woman presents with greenish frothy vaginal discharge, vulvovaginal irritation, and elevated vaginal pH. Amsel criteria and whiff test are negative. Wet mount examination is performed. Which of the following is the most likely morphology of the causative organism?

correctAnswer: A. Infection occurs by penetration of larvae through the skin
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The stool microscopy image is characteristic of hookworm ova (Ancylostoma duodenale or Necator americanus). Hookworm infection occurs when infective filariform larvae penetrate intact skin, commonly through bare feet exposed to contaminated soil. Chronic intestinal blood loss caused by hookworms can lead to iron deficiency anemia presenting with fatigue and pallor.

Hookworm infection:

  • Caused by Ancylostoma duodenale or Necator americanus.
  • Infective form is the filariform larva.
  • Transmission occurs by skin penetration.
  • Adult worms attach to the intestinal mucosa and feed on blood.

Microscopy findings:

  • Thin-shelled oval eggs.
  • Eggs contain segmented blastomeres.
  • Eggs of Ancylostoma and Necator are morphologically similar.

Important differentiating features of common helminths:

  • Hookworm - skin penetration, iron deficiency anaemia.
  • Ascaris lumbricoides - ingestion of eggs, intestinal obstruction.
  • Enterobius vermicularis - perianal itching, Scotch tape test positivity.

Infection occurs by ingestion of cysts in contaminated food (Option B): Seen in protozoal infections such as amoebiasis and giardiasis. Hookworms infect through larval skin penetration, not cyst ingestion.

The image represents eggs of Enterobius vermicularis (Option C): Enterobius eggs are planoconvex (“D-shaped”). Diagnosis is usually made by the Scotch tape test.

The parasite shown is Ascaris lumbricoides (Option D): Ascaris eggs are thick-shelled and mammillated. Infection occurs by ingestion of embryonated eggs.



Reference:

Paniker’s Textbook of Medical Parasitology, 8th Edition, Pages 187-189.

question: A young woman presents with fatigue and pallor. Stool microscopy reveals thin-shelled oval ova, as shown in the image. Which of the following statements regarding the parasite is correct?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The clinical presentation of bloody diarrhoea following travel to a tropical region, together with the histopathological finding of a characteristic flask-shaped colonic ulcer, is suggestive of invasive amoebic colitis caused by Entamoeba histolytica.

Amoebic Colitis

Causative organism

Entamoeba histolytica

Infective stage

Mature quadrinucleate cyst acquired by the fecal–oral route through contaminated food or water

Pathogenesis

Trophozoites invade the colonic mucosa and extend into the submucosa, producing characteristic flask-shaped ulcers

Histopathology

Flask-shaped ulcers with erythrophagocytic trophozoites located at the advancing margins of the ulcers

Common sites

Predominantly involves the cecum, sigmoid colon, and rectum

Clinical features

Bloody, mucus-containing diarrhoea (amoebic dysentery), abdominal pain, tenesmus, malaise, and weight loss; fever occurs in <40% of patients

Diagnosis
  • Demonstration of erythrophagocytic trophozoites in stool or biopsy is diagnostic
  • Stool antigen detection and PCR are highly sensitive and specific

Complications

Fulminant colitis, toxic megacolon, colonic perforation, and amoebic liver abscess containing sterile "anchovy paste" necrotic material

Cryptosporidiosis (Option A): Causes watery, non-bloody diarrhoea, particularly in immunocompromised individuals, and does not produce invasive colonic disease or flask-shaped ulcers.

Giardiasis (Option B): Primarily affects the small intestine, causing malabsorption with greasy, foul-smelling diarrhoea, rather than invasive colonic ulceration.

Cryptococcosis (Option C): An opportunistic fungal infection that most commonly causes meningitis and pulmonary disease in immunocompromised patients and is not associated with flask-shaped colonic ulcers.



Reference:

Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 1755-1757.
question: A 35-year-old man presents with abdominal pain, fever, and bloody diarrhea for the past week. He recently returned from a tropical region with poor sanitation. Histopathological examination of a colonic biopsy specimen is shown in the image below. What is the most likely causative organism?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Based on the patient's history of consuming undercooked pork and the presence of motile segments (proglottids) in the stool, the most likely causative organism is Taenia solium.

Intestinal taeniasis

Infection

Via consumption of undercooked infected meat of beef (T. saginata) (Option A) or pork (T. solium)

Clinical features

Despite their large size, adult worms cause little discomfort to the patient.

  • When symptoms do occur, they may include:
    • Vague abdominal discomfort
    • Indigestion
    • Nausea
    • Diarrhea
    • Weight loss
  • Rarely, complications such as acute intestinal obstruction, acute appendicitis, and pancreatitis occur.

Hymenolepis nana (Option B): This is the dwarf tapeworm, commonly seen in children and transmitted via the feco-oral route. It typically causes asymptomatic infection or mild GI symptoms and does not cause the passage of large motile segments in stool.

Enterobius vermicularis (Option C) causes pinworm infection, characterised by perianal itching, especially at night. Diagnosis is made by the tape test, and motile segments in stool are not seen.



Reference:
  1. Paniker’s Textbook of Medical Parasitology, 8th Edition, Pages 126,127
  2. https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/medicine-and-dentistry/cutaneous-amoebiasis#
question: A 40-year-old man presents with abdominal discomfort and passage of motile segments in the stool a few weeks after consuming undercooked pork. He has no fever or vomiting. Which is the most likely causative organism?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The image depicts stepwells surrounding a waterbody, which is the habitat for cyclops containing L3 larvae of Dracunculus medinensis that causes Guinea Worm disease (Dracunculiasis), and it was eliminated from India in February 2000 under the Guinea worm eradication programme, in which one of the methods of disease prevention includes converting stepwells to draw wells.

  • It is transmitted to humans through the ingestion of contaminated stagnant water containing L3 larva infected copepods (Cyclops), typically from ponds and stepwells.
  • The larvae are liberated in the stomach of humans, cross the duodenal wall, and enter the retroperitoneal connective tissues where they grow and mature into adults.
  • The males die after mating, and the females migrate in about six months to subcutaneous tissues, especially of legs, arms and back, which are likely to come in contact with water.

[[figure-1]]

These cases occur in areas that have natural or artificial ponds or step-wells as sources of drinking water. The chances of infection increase before the arrival of the monsoon when the water level becomes low in ponds/wells.

The prevention/control measures for Dracunculiasis include:

  • Making drinking water safe by not allowing villagers, especially those with blisters and ulcers, to enter any source of drinking water
  • Filtering water in endemic areas through a fine mesh (size 100 micrometres) to remove Cyclops
  • Converting step wells to draw wells
  • Controlling cyclops by the use of temephos
  • Increasing awareness among endemic communities about the disease and its control.

Whipworm (Option B): Trichuris trichiura, a large intestinal nematode, is acquired by ingestion of embryonated eggs containing infective rhabditiform larvae from soil-contaminated food. Hence, preventive measures include proper disposal of faeces and avoiding the consumption of unwashed fruits and vegetables.

[[figure-2]]

Hookworm (Option C): Hookworms (Ancylostoma duodenale and Necator americanus) are small intestinal nematodes that are transmitted via skin penetration by filariform larvae (L3) from contaminated soil when a person walks barefoot, and have no association with drinking water. The measures taken for prevention include proper disposal of faeces and the use of footwear.

[[figure-3]]

Roundworm (Option D): Ascaris lumbricoides, is a small intestinal nematode which spreads by ingestion of eggs from faecally contaminated food or soil, and is not linked to aquatic copepods. They can be eliminated by preventing faecal contamination of soil.

[[figure-4]]



Reference:
  1. Paniker's Textbook of Medical Parasitology, 8th Edition, Pages 225-229.
  2. https://ncdc.mohfw.gov.in/guinea-worm-eradication-programme/
question: A particular parasite commonly associated with water bodies, shown in the image, has been eliminated from this habitat. Which of the following parasites is it?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The presentation of a black necrotic lesion (eschar) surrounded by swelling and secondary vesicles is characteristic of cutaneous anthrax, which occurs when gram-positive Bacillus anthracis spores enter through damaged skin.
  • Commonly seen in dock workers carrying hides and skins on their bare backs. Also known as Hide-Porter’s disease.
  • The lesion is called a malignant pustule, as it starts as a papule 1-3 days after infection and becomes vesicular, containing fluid which may be clear or bloodstained with several satellite lesions. The whole area is congested and edematous and is covered by a black eschar.
  • Human anthrax is contracted from animals, and the disease may be:
    • a) cutaneous,
    • b) pulmonary,
    • c) intestinal,
      • All types lead to fatal septicemia or encephalopathy, and meningitis.

Feature Category

Characteristics of Bacillus anthracis

Gram Stain & Morphology

Gram-positive, large, boxcar-shaped bacilli/ Bamboo stick appearance

[[figure-1]]

Spore Formation

Spore-forming

Oxygen Requirement

Aerobic, Inverted fir tree appearance on stab culture

[[figure-2]]

Motility

Non-motile

Capsule

Polypeptide capsule with d(-) glutamic acid polymers

Virulence Factors / Exotoxins
  • Oedema Factor (EF): ↑ cAMP → massive oedema
  • Lethal Factor (LF): tissue necrosis and systemic toxicity

Colony Morphology (Culture)
  • Large (2 to 5 mm), grey, flat, non-hemolytic colonies with irregular margins, giving a frosted glass appearance.
  • Tenacious consistency firmly adheres to agar.
  • "Medusa head" appearance under the microscope.

[[figure-3]]

Other diseases where eschar is seen are:

  • Spotted fevers (Not in Rocky Mountain Spotted Fever)
  • Scrub typhus
  • Brown recluse spider bite.

Staphylococcus aureus (Option A): It is a gram-positive cocci that causes folliculitis, boils, furuncles, impetigo, echthyma, and cellulitis. It never presents with an eschar.

Clostridium perfringens (Option B): It is a gram-positive, spore-forming bacillus that causes food poisoning and gas gangrene when the spores enter traumatically and presents with severe pain, discharge, edema and crepitus.

Rickettsia conorii (Option C): It causes Indian tick typhus, which presents as fever, flu-like symptoms, and rash following a tick bite. "Tache noire" is the term for the eschar that classically develops with this disease and the lesions are painful, which differentiates it from the painless eschar seen in cutaneous anthrax.



Reference:
  1. Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology, 11th Edition, Page 233.
  2. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK560914/
question: A diabetic and hypertensive female presents with a painless ulcer over the leg with a characteristic black eschar at the centre, as shown in the image. There is surrounding oedema with minimal pain. Which of the following is the most likely causative organism?

correctAnswer: B. The graft survives because nude mice lack functional T lymphocytes
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Nude mice are genetically athymic, leading to a near-total deficiency in T-lymphocytes.
  • Because graft rejection is primarily a T cell-mediated process, these mice fail to reject grafts from other species (xenografts), making them invaluable for studying foreign tissues or tumors.


The graft is rapidly rejected due to a strong T-cell-mediated response (Option A): Nude mice lack T cells, so rapid T-cell-mediated rejection does not occur.


The graft is accepted permanently due to identical MHC molecules (Option C): Xenografts are between different species and do not share identical MHC.


The graft undergoes hyperacute rejection mediated by preformed antibodies (Option D): Hyperacute rejection is antibody-mediated and is not typical in nude mice.



Reference:
  1. Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology, 10th Edition, Page 132.
  2. https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0092867408006247

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

In the above scenario, TLR5 recognizes flagellin, the structural protein of bacterial flagella, and activates the innate immune response.

Innate immunity identifies microbes through Pattern Recognition Receptors (PRRs) located on the cell surface, endosomes, and in the cytoplasm, which recognize and bind Pathogen-Associated Molecular Patterns (PAMPs).

  • Toll-Like Receptors (TLRs): Membrane-bound receptors that induce cytokines (IL-1, IL-6, TNF-α).
    • Surface TLRs: detect extracellular components
    • Endosomal TLRs: detect nucleic acids from internalized pathogens.
  • Cytoplasmic Receptors: Detect intracellular pathogens and cellular stress.
    • C-type Lectin Receptors (CLRs): recognize microbial carbohydrates
    • NOD-like Receptors (NLRs): detect intracellular microbial products and stress; activate inflammasome → IL-1β
    • RIG-I-like Receptors (RLRs): detect viral RNA → induce type I interferons (IFN-α/β).
  • Phagocytic Receptors: Mediate attachment and uptake of microbes.
    • Opsonin receptors: bind coated pathogens
    • Scavenger receptors: bind microbial components.

Location

Cell Surface

question:
A patient presents with an acute bacterial infection. The organism identified is motile due to the presence of flagella (shown in the image), composed of flagellin, which activates the innate immune response.

Which of the following Toll-like receptors is primarily responsible for recognizing this microbial component?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Viral hemagglutination is a direct process where Hemagglutinin (HA) spikes on the surface of viruses like Influenza bind directly to receptors on red blood cells. This clumping is an inherent biological property of the virus and occurs without the need for an antibody-mediated reaction.

ELISA (Option A) is a labeled immunoassay that relies specifically on the binding of an antigen to an enzyme-linked antibody to produce a measurable color change.

Indirect hemagglutination (Option C): Also known as passive hemagglutination, this test requires specific antibodies to bridge red blood cells that have been artificially coated with antigens.

Western Blot (Option D) is a molecular technique used to detect specific proteins in a sample using gel electrophoresis and antibody marking, involving no direct microbial clumping of RBCs.

question: Which of the following processes describes the clumping of red blood cells (RBCs) caused by the direct action of microbial surface proteins rather than an antigen-antibody reaction?

correctAnswer: A. Protects against serogroups A, C, W-135, and Y, but not against B
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

MenACWY is a quadrivalent conjugate vaccine made from capsular polysaccharides of Neisseria meningitidis serogroups A, C, W-135, and Y, linked to a carrier protein. This linkage makes the immune response T-cell dependent, giving strong and long-lasting immunity.

Indications

  • Hypogammaglobulinemia (e.g., Bruton's agammaglobulinemia)
  • HIV infection
  • Elderly
  • Individuals living in high-endemic regions (e.g., Africa)
  • Asplenia / Splenectomy (risk for encapsulated organisms)
  • Terminal complement deficiency (C5-C9 MAC defects)

MenB Vaccine:

  • Targets Serogroup B, which MenACWY does NOT cover
  • Reason: Capsule mimics human neural cell adhesion molecule (NCAM) → poor immunogenicity
  • Protein-based:
    • Bexsero (4CMenB)
    • Trumenba (rLP2086)
  • Components:
    • Outer membrane proteins
    • Factor H binding protein.

Serogroup B → Its polysialic acid capsule mimics human NCAM, causing immune tolerance and poor antibody response, so protection requires protein-based MenB vaccines rather than capsule-based ones. (Option B, C ruled out)

Ineffective in adolescents due to poor T-cell response (Option D): Conjugate vaccines elicit a strong T-cell-dependent immune response and are highly effective in adolescents.



Reference:

Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology, 11th Edition, Page 220.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The child has the classic features of Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome (WAS):

  • Eczema
  • Recurrent bacterial infections
  • Thrombocytopenia (with small platelets)
  • Immunoglobulin pattern: ↓ IgM, normal/↑ IgG and IgA (often ↑IgE)
  • Absent isohemagglutinins due to poor response to polysaccharide antigens.

Patients with WAS have normal numbers of mature B cells, but B-cell function is defective because of abnormal T-cell help and intrinsic immune dysfunction.

Wiskott-Aldrich Syndrome (WAS)

  • Inheritance: X-linked recessive. (Option A ruled out)
  • Triad of features: Eczema, Thrombocytopenic purpura, Recurrent infections
  • Prognosis: Most affected boys rarely survive beyond the first decade, with death due to infection, hemorrhage, or lymphoreticular malignancy.
  • Cell-mediated immunity undergoes progressive deterioration, associated with thymic and paracortical lymph node depletion. (Option B ruled out)
  • Humoral immunity:
    • IgM levels: Low
    • IgG and IgA levels: Normal or elevated
    • Isohemagglutinins: Absent
    • Defect: Specific inability to respond to polysaccharide antigens. (Option D ruled out)
  • Gene: WAS gene located on Xp11.23
  • Protein: WASp (Wiskott-Aldrich Syndrome protein)
  • Function:
    • Regulates actin cytoskeleton remodeling in hematopoietic cells
    • Essential for:
      • Immune synapse formation
      • T-cell activation
      • B-cell function
      • Platelet formation
  • Defect leads to:
    • Combined immunodeficiency + thrombocytopenia.

Explanation:

  • The given scenario, with features of drooping eyelids and facial weakness, as shown in the image, along with proximal muscle weakness, suggests Myasthenia Gravis, a classic example of a Type II (antibody-mediated) hypersensitivity reaction caused by IgG autoantibodies targeting acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction.

Type II hypersensitivity reactions: Antibodies target cell-surface or receptor antigens, causing blockade, stimulation, or destruction.

Examples include:

  • Myasthenia Gravis: blocks ACh receptors → weakness
  • Graves’ Disease: stimulates TSH receptors → hyperthyroidism
  • Some forms of Type 1 Diabetes: antibodies affect insulin receptor function.

Rheumatoid arthritis (RA):

  • Predominantly Type III hypersensitivity → immune complex deposition (RF, anti-CCP)
  • Also has components of:
    • Type II hypersensitivity → antibody-mediated cellular effects
    • Type IV hypersensitivity → T-cell mediated synovial inflammation

Therefore:

  • RA is not a pure Type II antireceptor disease, but it is also not exclusively Type III
  • Hence, not a perfect single-best example, but still considered incorrect in this context

Type I - Immediate (IgE-mediated) (Option A): Involves IgE antibodies and mast cell degranulation, causing allergic reactions like asthma or urticaria, not receptor-targeted autoimmunity.

Type III - Immune complex-mediated (Option C): Caused by deposition of antigen-antibody complexes in tissues (e.g., serum sickness, SLE), not by antibodies targeting cell-surface receptors.

Type IV - Delayed (T-cell mediated) (Option D): Mediated by sensitized T cells over 24-72 hours, such as in contact dermatitis or tuberculin reaction, not by IgG antibodies at the neuromuscular junction.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Secondary mediators are newly synthesized after mast cell activation, primarily derived from arachidonic acid via the cyclooxygenase and lipoxygenase pathways. They include:

  • Prostaglandins (Option B)
  • Leukotrienes (Option B)
  • TNF-α
  • IL-4

Type I Hypersensitivity Pathway (Stepwise):

1) First Exposure (Sensitization Phase):

  • Allergen enters body → taken up by APCs (dendritic cells)
  • Presented to CD4+ T cells → differentiation into Th2 cells
  • Th2 cells release:
    • IL-4, IL-13 → B cell class switching to IgE
  • Plasma cells produce IgE antibodies
  • IgE binds to FcεRI receptors on mast cells and basophils
  • Mast cells become sensitized (coated with IgE)

2) Re-Exposure (Effector Phase):

  • Same allergen re-enters
  • Cross-links IgE on mast cell surface
  • Leads to mast cell degranulation

3) Mediator Release:

A. Primary (Preformed) Mediators:

  • Histamine
  • Tryptase
  • Heparin

B. Secondary (Newly Synthesized) Mediators:

  • Prostaglandins (PGD₂)
  • Leukotrienes (LTC₄, LTD₄, LTE₄)
  • Cytokines (TNF-α, IL-4, IL-5)

4) Clinical Effects:

  • Vasodilation → redness
  • Increased vascular permeability → edema
  • Bronchoconstriction → wheeze
  • Mucus secretion → rhinorrhea

Histamine and tryptase (Option A) are primary mediators, pre-formed in granules.

IgE and IgG antibodies (Option C) are antibodies, not mediators released from mast cells.

Complement proteins C3 and C5 (Option D) are part of innate immunity, not secondary mediators in Type I hypersensitivity.

Type II - Antibody-mediated (Option B): Involves IgG or IgM antibodies targeting cells or tissues, causing cytotoxicity, not IgE-mediated mast cell activation.

Type IV - Delayed (T-cell mediated) (Option D): Mediated by sensitized T cells over 24-72 hours, not by IgE or immediate mast cell degranulation.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

In humans, the Major Histocompatibility Complex (MHC) is synonymous with the Human Leukocyte Antigen (HLA) system.

  • These genes are tightly clustered on the short arm (p) of chromosome 6.
  • They are inherited together as a haplotype, which is why HLA typing is critical for transplant compatibility.
  • The MHC gene complex consists of three clusters:
    • Class I (A, B, C loci)
    • Class II (DR, DQ, DP loci)
    • Class III (complement region)

Major Histocompatibility Complex (MHC) / HLA Complex

Primary Function

Recognition and elimination of foreign cells and antigens. It is responsible for the rejection of allografts (tissues/organs from another member of the same species).

Classes of Proteins
  • Class I Proteins: Class II Proteins: Regulate the immune response.
  • Class III Proteins: Include components of the complement system (C2, C4), properdin factor B, heat shock proteins, and Tumor Necrosis Factors (TNF alpha and beta).

MHC Loci and Molecules
  • HLA Class I: Comprises A, B, and C loci. These molecules consist of a heavy peptide chain (alpha chain) non-covalently linked to beta2-microglobulin (coded on chromosome 15). They are found on the surface of virtually all nucleated cells and present antigens to CD8 T cells.
  • HLA Class II: Includes DR, DQ, and DP loci. These are heterodimers (alpha and beta chains) restricted to antigen-presenting cells (macrophages, dendritic cells, B cells). They present antigens to CD4 T cells and are primarily responsible for graft-versus-host response and mixed leukocyte reaction (MLR).

Features
  • Pleomorphism: The HLA system is highly pleomorphic; for example, at least 24 distinct alleles have been identified at the HLA locus A and 50 at the locus B.
  • MHC Restriction: T cells only recognize antigens when presented as a complex with the MHC molecule.

Significance

Critical for transplantation compatibility and protecting against microbial infections.



Reference:

Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology, 10th Edition, Page 141-142.

question: A 32-year-old male awaiting a kidney transplant is being HLA typed to match donor and recipient MHC antigens. The gene cluster responsible for encoding these HLA antigens is located on which of the following chromosomal sites?

correctAnswer: B. They cannot self-replicate and must be integrated into a host DNA molecule
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Transposons or jumping genes are DNA segments that move within the genome but cannot replicate independently; they must integrate into a host DNA molecule to propagate.

Transposons or Jumping Genes

Definition

Transposable genetic elements → structurally and genetically discrete segments of DNA that can move around in a "cut-and-paste" manner between chromosomal and extrachromosomal DNA molecules within cells.

Structure

A transposon is a segment of DNA containing one or more genes in the center, flanked by inverted repeat sequences at both ends. These are nucleotide sequences that are complementary to each other but in reverse order.

Loop Formation

Due to the inverted repeats, single strands of a transposon can form a single-stranded loop carrying the gene, with a double-stranded stem formed by hydrogen bonding between the terminal inverted repeat sequences.

Types

  • Insertion Sequences (IS): Small transposons (1–2 kb) that carry only the genetic information necessary for transposition.
  • Complex/Composite Transposons: Larger segments that carry additional genes (such as those for antibiotic resistance) flanked by IS elements.

Movement

Transposons attach to certain regions of chromosomal, plasmid, or phage DNA. Unlike plasmids, they are not self-replicating and depend entirely on the host's chromosomal or plasmid DNA for replication.

Genetic Impact

The insertion of a transposon leads to the acquisition of new characteristics by the recipient DNA molecule. They utilize transposase enzymes to recognize the inverted repeated sequences for the "jumping" process.

[[figure-1]]

They are independent replicons that can replicate without a host genome (Option A): Transposons are not independent replicons; they cannot replicate on their own.

They are exclusively found in eukaryotic cells and are absent in bacteria (Option C): Transposons are found in both prokaryotes and eukaryotes, not just eukaryotes.

They move between cells only through the process of translation (Option D): Transposons move within the genome, not between cells via translation.



Reference:

Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology, 10th Edition, Page 63

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

MHC Class I molecules are expressed on all nucleated cells and present endogenous antigens to CD8⁺ cytotoxic T cells, playing a central role in allograft rejection and cell-mediated cytolysis.

  • HLA Class I molecules consist of a heavy alpha (α) chain non-covalently associated with a smaller peptide called β2-microglobulin (β chain).

[[figure-1]]

Graft Immunology

Graft Types and Recognition
  • Allografts: Tissues or organs grafted from one individual to another member of the same species. These are recognized as foreign and rejected by the immune system.
  • MHC Role: The primary function of the MHC (HLA in humans) is the recognition and elimination of foreign cells. Antigens responsible for allograft rejection are called alloantigens, found on the surface of leukocytes.

Graft Rejection
  • MHC Class I Involvement: Class I molecules (HLA-A, B, and C) determine histocompatibility. They are primarily involved in cell-mediated cytolysis and the acceptance or rejection of allografts.
  • Mechanism: CD8+ cytotoxic T cells recognize foreign Class I MHC molecules on the graft, leading to the destruction of the target cells.
  • Effector Mechanisms: Activated macrophages (stimulated by lymphokines or interferon) play an important role in antitumor activity and graft rejection.

Graft-versus-Host (GvH) Disease
  • MHC Class II Involvement: HLA Class II molecules (DR, DQ, and DP) are primarily responsible for the graft-versus-host response.
  • Mechanism: In GvH, immunocompetent T cells within the grafted tissue recognize the recipient's (host) MHC antigens as foreign and mount an immune attack against the host's tissues.
  • Mixed Leukocyte Reaction (MLR): Class II molecules are the major determinants that trigger the proliferation of T cells in an MLR, which is used to predict GvH and rejection potential.

MHC Class II (Option B) presents exogenous antigens to CD4⁺ T cells.

MHC Class III (Option C) encodes complement proteins and cytokines.

MHC Class IV (Option D) does not exist.



Reference:

Bruton's agammaglobulinemia (X-linked agammaglobulinemia) is a B-cell immunodeficiency characterized by a failure of B-cell maturation and a resultant lack of antibodies.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Pepsin cleaves immunoglobulin below the hinge region, producing an F(ab’)₂ fragment composed of two Fab portions held together. Mercaptoethanol reduces disulfide bonds and separates heavy and light chains. Papain cleaves above the hinge region, producing two Fab fragments and one Fc fragment.

[[figure-1]]

Immunoglobulin structure:

  • Immunoglobulins are glycoproteins composed of:
    • Two heavy chains
    • Two light chains
  • Chains are linked by disulfide bonds.

Enzymatic cleavage of antibodies:

  • Pepsin:
    • Cleaves below the hinge region
    • Produces:
      • One F(ab’)₂ fragment
    • Fc portion is degraded.
  • Papain:
    • Cleaves above the hinge region
    • Produces:
      • Two Fab fragments
      • One Fc fragment.
  • Mercaptoethanol:
    • Acts as a reducing agent
    • Cleaves disulfide bonds separating antibody subunits.

Functions of antibody fragments:

  • Fab fragment:
    • Responsible for antigen binding
  • Fc fragment:
    • Mediates complement activation and Fc receptor binding
  • F(ab’)₂ fragment:
    • Retains bivalent antigen-binding capacity

Important concepts:

  • Heavy chains determine immunoglobulin class
  • Variable regions bind antigen
  • Constant regions mediate effector functions


Reference:

Ananthanarayan and Paniker’s Textbook of Microbiology, 11th Edition, Pages 104-106

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

ESBLs (Extended-Spectrum β-Lactamases) are enzymes produced mainly by gram-negative organisms such as Escherichia coli and Klebsiella pneumoniae. These enzymes hydrolyse penicillins, cephalosporins, and aztreonam.

  • Carbapenems are the most reliable treatment for serious ESBL infections.
  • ESBL genes are commonly plasmid-mediated, facilitating rapid spread of resistance.
  • Piperacillin-tazobactam may be used in selected susceptible low-risk infections.

Important microbiological features of ESBLs:

  • Commonly plasmid-mediated
  • Cause resistance to:
    • Penicillins
    • Third-generation cephalosporins
    • Aztreonam
  • Usually inhibited by β-lactamase inhibitors such as clavulanic acid

Common ESBL-producing organisms:

  • Escherichia coli
  • Klebsiella pneumoniae

Treatment principles:

  • Carbapenems:
    • Drugs of choice for severe invasive ESBL infections
    • Resistant to ESBL-mediated hydrolysis
  • Piperacillin-tazobactam:
    • May be considered in selected mild or low-inoculum infections if susceptibility is confirmed
    • Less preferred in severe sepsis or bacteremia

Clinical importance:

  • Common causes of:
    • Urinary tract infections
    • Sepsis
    • Pneumonia
    • Intra-abdominal infections
  • Associated with multidrug resistance and treatment failure

First-generation cephalosporins are hydrolysed by ESBL enzymes and are ineffective against ESBL-producing organisms (Statement 4)



Reference:

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Transduction refers to phage-mediated genetic recombination in bacteria, wherein a bacteriophage transfers bacterial genetic material from a donor to a recipient cell. In its simplest form, a transducing particle consists of bacterial nucleic acid encapsulated within a phage-derived protein coat.

Types of Transduction

1. Generalised Transduction

In generalised transduction, any segment of donor bacterial DNA may be transferred.
The DNA incorporated into the transducing phage is random, without preference for specific genetic loci. This typically results from packaging errors during phage assembly, where fragments of the bacterial chromosome are mistakenly enclosed within the phage capsid.

2. Restricted (Specialised) Transduction

Restricted transduction involves the transfer of only specific genetic traits. This occurs when a bacteriophage integrates into a defined site of the bacterial chromosome and excises imprecisely, carrying adjacent host genes along with it.

A classic example is observed with the λ (lambda) phage of Escherichia coli.

[[figure-1]]

Transformation (Option B): Uptake of naked DNA from the environment by competent bacteria (e.g., Streptococcus pneumoniae). It does not involve a bacteriophage.

[[figure-2]]

Conjugation (Option C): Requires direct cell-to-cell contact via an F pilus transferring plasmids (e.g., F+ → F−). No viral particle is involved.

[[figure-3]]

Transposition (Option D): Movement of mobile genetic elements (transposons) within or between DNA molecules. Does not require bacteriophages or cell contact.

[[figure-4]]



Reference:

Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology, 11th Edition, Pages 56-58.
